# Overview

This report completes the six tasks in **Part 1** using the supplied already-cleaned `listings_clean.rds` dataset. The original CSV cleaning steps are intentionally not repeated, so results reflect the provided RDS data.

**Tasks:** (1) price by room type; (2) bedroom distribution; (3) price versus review score; (4) property-type distribution; (5) top 10 neighbourhoods table; (6) top 10 neighbourhoods chart.

# Step 1 — Setup and load the dataset

```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = TRUE, warning = FALSE, message = FALSE)
```

```{r load-data}
# Import libraries needed for cleaning, plotting and table formatting.
library(tidyverse)
library(knitr)

# Put listings_clean.rds in the same folder as this Rmd.
# RDS files preserve R column classes and factor levels.
listings_clean <- readRDS("listings_clean.rds")

# Examine the imported data.
glimpse(listings_clean)
```

# Step 2 — Check the cleaned RDS variables

The file `listings_clean.rds` is already a cleaned dataset. **Do not reapply the CSV filters from the earlier lab**, since doing so could unnecessarily remove observations. First, confirm that all required variables exist and that numeric variables can be plotted.

```{r prepare-data}
# Copy the RDS dataset, leaving the original object unchanged.
listings <- listings_clean

# Make sure the six exercises' required fields are present.
required_vars <- c(
  "price", "room_type", "bedrooms", "review_scores_rating",
  "property_type", "neighbourhood_cleansed"
)
missing_vars <- setdiff(required_vars, names(listings))
if (length(missing_vars) > 0) {
  stop("Missing columns in listings_clean.rds: ",
       paste(missing_vars, collapse = ", "))
}

# Check types; the already-cleaned file should have numeric prices and ratings.
if (!is.numeric(listings$price) ||
    !is.numeric(listings$review_scores_rating)) {
  stop("price and review_scores_rating must be numeric. Check the RDS columns.")
}

cat("Number of listings in RDS:", nrow(listings), "\n")
print(sapply(listings[required_vars], class))
print(count(listings, room_type, sort = TRUE))
```

# Step 3 — Task 1: Boxplot of price by room type

**Question:** How does `price` vary between `room_type` categories?

Each box shows the median and middle 50% of prices; points beyond the whiskers are potential outliers.

```{r task-1-boxplot, fig.width=9, fig.height=5}
task1_plot <- listings %>%
  filter(!is.na(room_type)) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = room_type, y = price)) +
  geom_boxplot(fill = "skyblue", alpha = 0.8) +
  labs(
    title = "Airbnb Prices by Room Type in Edinburgh",
    subtitle = "Based on the supplied cleaned RDS dataset",
    x = "Room type",
    y = "Price (dataset currency)",
    caption = "Source: Edinburgh Airbnb listings dataset"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

print(task1_plot)
```

# Step 4 — Task 2: Distribution of bedrooms

**Question:** How many listings have 0, 1, 2, 3, etc. bedrooms?

The bedroom count is discrete, so a bar chart is appropriate.

```{r task-2-bedrooms, fig.width=9, fig.height=5}
task2_plot <- listings %>%
  filter(!is.na(bedrooms)) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = factor(bedrooms))) +
  geom_bar(fill = "steelblue") +
  labs(
    title = "Distribution of Bedrooms Among Airbnb Listings",
    x = "Number of bedrooms",
    y = "Number of listings"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

print(task2_plot)

# Optional frequency table for checking the chart.
listings %>% count(bedrooms, sort = TRUE)
```

# Step 5 — Task 3: Relationship between price and review score

**Question:** Is there a relationship between `price` and `review_scores_rating`?

Each point is a listing. Jitter and transparency help when listings overlap. The fitted line shows a linear trend; it does not demonstrate causation.

```{r task-3-scatter, fig.width=9, fig.height=5}
task3_plot <- listings %>%
  filter(!is.na(review_scores_rating)) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = review_scores_rating, y = price)) +
  geom_jitter(alpha = 0.2, width = 0.1, height = 0) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = TRUE, colour = "red") +
  labs(
    title = "Airbnb Price and Review Score",
    x = "Review score rating",
    y = "Price (dataset currency)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

print(task3_plot)
```

# Step 6 — Task 4: Distribution of property types

**Question:** Which `property_type` categories are most common?

Horizontal bars help display long category names. The most common types appear at the top.

```{r task-4-property-types, fig.width=10, fig.height=7}
task4_plot <- listings %>%
  filter(!is.na(property_type)) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = forcats::fct_rev(forcats::fct_infreq(property_type)))) +
  geom_bar(fill = "steelblue") +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(
    title = "Distribution of Airbnb Property Types",
    x = "Property type",
    y = "Number of listings"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

print(task4_plot)
```

# Step 7 — Task 5: Top 10 neighbourhoods table

**Question:** Which ten neighbourhoods have the largest number of listings?

We count listings, sort from highest to lowest and retain the first ten.

```{r task-5-top10-table}
top10_neighbourhoods <- listings %>%
  filter(!is.na(neighbourhood_cleansed)) %>%
  count(neighbourhood_cleansed, name = "number_of_listings") %>%
  arrange(desc(number_of_listings), neighbourhood_cleansed) %>%
  slice_head(n = 10)

knitr::kable(
  top10_neighbourhoods,
  col.names = c("Neighbourhood", "Number of listings"),
  caption = "Top 10 Edinburgh neighbourhoods by Airbnb listing count"
)
```

# Step 8 — Task 6: Plot the top 10 neighbourhoods

**Question:** How do listing counts compare across the top ten neighbourhoods?

We reuse the table created in Task 5, so both outputs show the same neighbourhoods and counts.

```{r task-6-top10-chart, fig.width=10, fig.height=6}
task6_plot <- top10_neighbourhoods %>%
  ggplot(aes(
    x = reorder(neighbourhood_cleansed, number_of_listings),
    y = number_of_listings
  )) +
  geom_col(fill = "skyblue") +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(
    title = "Top 10 Edinburgh Neighbourhoods by Airbnb Listings",
    x = "Neighbourhood",
    y = "Number of listings"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

print(task6_plot)
```

# Step 9 — Checklist and optional export

All six tasks are represented above: **five plots and one table**. The export commands below are optional and only run when you change `eval=FALSE` to `eval=TRUE`.

```{r export-outputs, eval=FALSE}
ggsave("Task1_Price_by_RoomType.png", task1_plot, width = 9, height = 5, dpi = 300)
ggsave("Task2_Bedrooms.png", task2_plot, width = 9, height = 5, dpi = 300)
ggsave("Task3_Price_vs_Reviews.png", task3_plot, width = 9, height = 5, dpi = 300)
ggsave("Task4_Property_Types.png", task4_plot, width = 10, height = 7, dpi = 300)
ggsave("Task6_Top10_Neighbourhoods.png", task6_plot, width = 10, height = 6, dpi = 300)
write_csv(top10_neighbourhoods, "Task5_Top10_Neighbourhoods.csv")
```

**To create the HTML report:** Open this `.Rmd` in RStudio, put `listings_clean.rds` in the same folder (or update its path), then click **Knit → Knit to HTML**.
